title: The Year of Four Emperors: Bedriacum, Otho and the Rise of Vespasian
sum: Book 2 begins far from Rome, with Vespasian's son Titus turning back from his road to the new emperor, and it ends with the East ready to follow Vespasian. In between, Otho's armies and Vitellius's armies fight along the Padus. Vitellius's men win at Bedriacum, Otho refuses to fight on and kills himself, and Vitellius takes Rome and quickly loses the respect of his own soldiers.

The Jewish war and the Bible's world sit at the edges of the book. Tacitus describes the temple of Venus at Paphos and the altar on Mount Carmel, names Caesarea, Antioch and Alexandria, and says that King Agrippa and Queen Berenice backed Vespasian. His account of how a general in Judea became emperor, with Mucianus's speech and a quick oath of the legions, sets up everything that happens to Jerusalem in Book 5.
readings: Book 2 is a record of how armies, not the Senate, now made emperors: Otho's soldiers choose to fight, Vitellius's soldiers make him, and Vespasian's soldiers hail him as he steps out of his room. Tacitus writes it as a lesson in what power does to those who hold it.

The same provinces, cities and people are in Acts and the Gospels: Corinth, Paphos, Caesarea, Antioch, Alexandria, King Agrippa, Bernice, centurions and tribunes. Jesus's words about 'wars and reports of wars' (Matthew 24:6) and the siege of Jerusalem (Luke 21:20) are the background to what Tacitus says is left for Titus to do.

views.C: A Christian reader sees the Roman year of four emperors as the world Jesus described: "You are going to hear of wars and reports of wars" (Matthew 24:6). Tacitus's diagnosis of civil war, an old craving for power, is the one James gives for every war (James 4:1-2). At the center of the book are places and people the New Testament knows: Agrippa and Bernice, who sat at Paul's hearing (Acts 25:13); Paphos, where Paul met Sergius Paulus (Acts 13:6-12); Caesarea (Acts 10:1) and Antioch (Acts 11:26); and Mount Carmel, where the people threw themselves down and said, "The LORD, he is the God!" (1 Kings 18:39). Tacitus sees none of this; he reports omens read in entrails and trees. Paul and Peter tell Christians to honor rulers (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13-14) even in a year like this, and Christians differ on what Rome's fall into civil war means for the end (see the pages on the Olivet Discourse, Rome and Nero).
views.H: The Histories were written about AD 100-110, a generation after these events (Wikipedia, "Histories (Tacitus)"). Book 2 names few sources: some authors who thought the armies might have chosen peace (2:37), common report about the bird at Otho's death (2:50), and the writers who recorded the war under the Flavians (2:101). Plutarch and Suetonius agree with Tacitus on Otho's death by dagger and on the battle at Bedriacum, and Suetonius agrees on the astrologers and the cypress omen. They differ on details such as Otho's age, the day of the Judean oath and whose land the cypress stood on. Josephus differs on the order in which Vespasian was proclaimed. The Wikipedia article on the year lists the ancient sources and the modern historians who work on it, including Ronald H. Martin (1981) and Gwyn Morgan (2006); it quotes Morgan's judgment that Verginius Rufus was "a mediocrity" who was out of his depth (Morgan 2006, pp. 22-24).
views.R: The first readers knew the machinery: the Praetorian Guard that kept the emperor, the legions with their numbers and nicknames, Roman Knights who ran provinces such as Egypt, the Senate that voted honors it did not choose, and the gladiator shows that Tacitus finds low even for soldiers. They also knew the titles: Caesar, Augustus, imperator and chief priest. Book 2 shows each in use: Vitellius refuses the names and keeps the power (2:62); Vespasian's soldiers pile them on (2:80). Omens fill the story, from the entrails at Paphos to the astrologers driven out of Italy. Tacitus tells them with distance.
views.J: Josephus tells these months in Jewish War 4: the soldiers of Judea proclaim Vespasian, Mucianus and Tiberius Alexander back him, he frees Josephus because Josephus had foretold the throne, and Titus is sent against Jerusalem. Tacitus and Josephus agree on the people and the outcome, and differ on whether Vespasian refused at first and on which oath came first. Suetonius tells the cypress and the Carmel oracle in Vespasian 5. Acts shows the Herod family, governors and centurions of the same province. The people named in both Tacitus's Book 2 and the New Testament are Agrippa II, Berenice, and the emperors Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius, plus the places named in the notes. Rabbinic tradition has its own story of Vespasian's rise: in the Babylonian Talmud (Gittin 56b, a later story) Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai tells Vespasian "you are a king" and reads Isaiah 10:34, about Lebanon falling to a mighty one, as a sign that the Temple would fall to a king. It is a Jewish counterpart to the prophecy stories in Josephus and Suetonius at 2:78 and 2:80.

deep.title: Two Carmel guesses
deep.b: Claude's theory: Tacitus's Carmel is a place where two memories meet. Greek-speaking people had a god of Carmel (the inscription to Zeus of Carmel, Wikipedia), and the mountain still held the memory of the altar that Elijah mended (1 Kings 18:30). The bare altar Tacitus describes could come from either. The Wikipedia article on Mount Carmel also says the mountain was a major center for the storm god Hadad, the Baal of 1 Kings 18:19-40, which is the setting of Elijah's contest. The link from Tacitus's altar to Elijah's is Claude's own: the only Elijah-altar statement in that article is that a monastery altar is claimed to be his, which it calls unlikely. The evidence for the link is only that an altar without a statue is what Israel's God allows.

echoes: Matthew 24:6-7; Luke 21:20-24; Luke 21:5-6; Acts 13:4-13; Acts 25:13-26:32; Acts 10:1; Acts 11:26; 1 Kings 18:19-40; Daniel 4:26; 1 Samuel 31:4; Revelation 13:3; Revelation 17:9-11; James 4:1-2; 1 Corinthians 4:9; Philippians 1:13

settings.by: Titus Vespasian, as Tacitus reports him
settings.to: a few friends he called in at Corinth
settings.when: as he learned that Galba was dead and that Vitellius was in arms
settings.why: To decide whether to go on to Rome or turn back. He weighs being a hostage to Vitellius or Otho against giving offense to the winner, and concludes that his father's joining one side will excuse a son. Tacitus gives these words in direct speech, so the wording is his.

settings.by: Sostratus, priest of Venus at Paphos
settings.to: Titus, in public and then in a private meeting
settings.when: after Titus sacrificed and asked, in roundabout words, about himself
settings.why: To tell Titus that the goddess approved 'some great enterprise.' Tacitus gives only the public answer in outline and says the priest 'laid out the future' in private; what he said is not recorded.

settings.by: the eastern generals, as Tacitus reports them
settings.to: each other (told in indirect speech)
settings.when: as the troops in the East grew eager for war while Otho and Vitellius fought
settings.why: To justify staying out of the civil war for now: winners and losers never truly join in good faith, and the soldiers' indiscipline, laziness and luxury would ruin one rival by war and the other by victory. Tacitus adds that the generals' real motives differed, from love of the state to hunger for plunder.

settings.what: The pretender's appeal to the ship captains
settings.to: the captains of two warships from Misenum
settings.when: when Calpurnius Asprenas came to catch him
settings.why: To get a passage to Syria or Egypt by pleading for the loyalty of old soldiers. The captains said they must speak to their men and would return; they reported everything to Asprenas, and the ship was taken.

settings.by: the people of Corsica, as Tacitus reports them
settings.to: each other, after Pacarius began drafting men
settings.when: when the procurator Pacarius forced an oath to Vitellius and a draft
settings.why: To reject a pointless war: 'We live on an island, and Germany... [is] far away.' It turned a forced oath into a plot, and they killed Pacarius in the bath.

settings.what: The soldiers' cry that Otho is betrayed
settings.to: their commander Spurinna
settings.when: as Caecina approached and Spurinna wanted to stay inside the walls
settings.why: To force a sortie. They shouted that Otho was being betrayed and that Caecina had been invited in, and pointed their weapons at the commander who tried to stop them.

settings.what: The legions' protest at losing the Batavians
settings.to: Valens and each other
settings.when: when Valens ordered part of the Batavians to relieve Gallia Narbonensis
settings.why: To keep their strongest troops: 'You can't tear the strongest limbs off the body.' It began the riot in which Valens hid in disguise (2:29).

settings.to: Valens, as they chased him and searched his tent
settings.when: during the riot over the Batavians
settings.why: To accuse Valens of hiding the plunder of Gaul and the gold of the people of Vienna, pay they thought they had earned. They threw stones, tore apart his baggage and probed his tent with javelins, until the camp prefect Alfenus Varus stopped the sentries' rounds and the trumpet calls and the mutiny died down.

settings.what: Letters of insult between the generals
settings.to: Otho
settings.when: after Valens's army marched from Ticinum and joined Caecina's
settings.why: To heap abuse on Otho while Otho's side, though it had 'plenty of material for abuse,' held back. Tacitus uses the contrast to show who was behaving better.

settings.to: Otho and his council, at Otho's request
settings.when: when Otho held a discussion on whether to drag the war out or try his luck
settings.why: To persuade Otho to wait: Vitellius's army has no supplies, Gaul may rise, and the Moesian troops are coming. The case fails (2:33). Tacitus gives these words in direct speech, so the wording is his.

settings.what: Titianus and Proculus talk Otho into Brixellum
settings.by: Titianus and Proculus, Otho's brother and Praetorian prefect
settings.to: Otho
settings.when: after the decision to fight was made
settings.why: To get Otho out of the battle "to save himself for the highest matters and for ruling." Paullinus and Celsus stopped arguing because they did not want to seem to put the emperor in danger. Tacitus says the day crushed Otho's cause, since a strong force of his guards left with him.

settings.to: his readers
settings.when: as he stops the story to ask whether the armies might have chosen peace
settings.why: To say that he does not think the soldiers or commanders would have accepted peace, and to trace civil war to a human craving for power from Marius and Sulla to AD 69.

settings.to: his generals Titianus and Proculus
settings.when: as the army set out toward the meeting of the Padus and the Arda
settings.why: To end delay and 'bring things to a decision.' It overrode Celsus and Paullinus, who had protested against marching tired troops at the enemy.

settings.by: the Praetorian soldiers of Otho's army
settings.to: each other and Otho's officers
settings.when: after the defeat, in the camp at Bedriacum
settings.why: To refuse to count the loss as final: 'we'd die more honorably in battle.' It shows what Otho could still have done (2:46).

settings.by: Plotius Firmus, prefect of the Praetorian Guard
settings.to: Otho
settings.when: after reports of defeat, with soldiers clinging to Otho
settings.why: To persuade Otho to fight on: 'It takes more courage to bear misfortune than to be rid of it.' Otho refuses (2:47). Tacitus gives these words in direct speech, so the wording is his.

settings.what: Otho's last speech to the soldiers
settings.to: the soldiers and officers around him
settings.when: the evening after the defeat
settings.why: To explain why he will not renew the war: he will not risk 'this spirit and courage' again, will not let more young Romans die, and says that blaming gods or men is for someone who wants to live. Plutarch gives the same thought in different words (Otho 15). Tacitus gives these words in direct speech, so the wording is his.

settings.to: Salvius Cocceianus, his brother's son, a very young man
settings.when: as he sent everyone away
settings.why: To calm the boy's fear: Vitellius will return the favor, and Otho is the first to bring the throne into a new family. Plutarch also has Otho comfort his nephew Cocceius (Otho 16.2).

settings.to: the ringleaders of the soldiers' uproar, and the friends who were leaving
settings.when: the evening and night before his death
settings.why: To end the tumult and get everyone away safely: he scolded the ringleaders and spent his time speaking with those who were leaving until all had gone unharmed. Tacitus does not give his words.

settings.what: Licinius Caecina's attack on Eprius Marcellus
settings.to: Eprius Marcellus and the senators gathered at Mutina
settings.when: when the senators, stranded after Otho's defeat, quarreled
settings.why: To make a name by attacking a big enemy: he blamed Marcellus for speaking ambiguously. Better men broke up the quarrel.

settings.to: his soldiers
settings.when: when he heard of the victory at Bedriacum on the road
settings.why: To praise the army's courage; he refused the army's request to make Asiaticus a Knight in public and gave him the rings at a private dinner.

settings.what: Mariccus's claim to be a god
settings.to: the Aedui villages and the 8,000 men who followed him
settings.when: early in Vitellius's reign
settings.why: To raise a following by proclaiming himself 'champion of Gaul and a god.' the Aedui, with cohorts Vitellius added, crushed it, and the crowd's belief in his invulnerability ended when he was killed before Vitellius.

settings.to: the people of Rome and the Senate
settings.when: as he came toward the city
settings.why: To put off the name Augustus, refuse the name Caesar, keep real power, expel the astrologers from Italy and forbid Roman Knights to disgrace themselves in the gladiator school and the arena.

settings.to: those around her, reading his first letters
settings.when: when Vitellius took the name Germanicus in his letters
settings.why: To say that she had given birth to Vitellius, not a Germanicus, and to show her distance from the new family's pride.

settings.to: Vespasian, in front of the other legates and friends
settings.when: after many private talks, while Vespasian wavered
settings.why: To persuade Vespasian to take the throne: the state would gain, Vitellius is weak, the East has nine legions, and Mucianus will be his partner and not rival. The first of the two verses is addressed to Vespasian; the second is Mucianus's own pledge. Tacitus gives these words in direct speech, so the wording is his.
views: The speech is Tacitus's account. Josephus has the commanders and Mucianus urge Vespasian after the soldiers' acclamation (Jewish War 4.10), and Suetonius mentions only that Mucianus promised the Syrian army (Vespasian 6.4); neither gives a speech. So the order (speech first) and the wording are Tacitus's.

settings.by: Basilides, priest of the god of Carmel
settings.to: Vespasian, as he sacrificed
settings.when: as Vespasian turned his secret hopes over in his mind
settings.why: To tell Vespasian that whatever he planned, he was being given a great dwelling, huge boundaries and many men. Rumor made it public, and people spelled it out as the throne.

settings.to: the people of Antioch in the theater, and the Syrian soldiers
settings.when: after the soldiers hailed Vespasian as emperor
settings.why: To stir the province and the army by claiming that Vitellius meant to swap the German and Syrian legions, giving the Syrians the harsh German winter camps.

settings.to: all the armies and legates, who were told to invite the Praetorians hostile to Vitellius
settings.when: as the East armed for war
settings.why: To invite the Praetorians to come over with the prize of renewed service. Tacitus does not give the text.

settings.what: Vitellius's speech to the Senate and people
settings.to: the Senate and people, the day after he entered Rome
settings.when: the day after he entered the city
settings.why: To praise his own energy and self-control. Tacitus says the people knew better, applauded anyway, and pushed him to take the name Augustus.

settings.to: friends calming him after Helvidius Priscus spoke against his wishes
settings.when: after the praetor-elect Helvidius Priscus opposed him in the Senate
settings.why: To say it was nothing new for two senators to disagree in a free republic, and that he too had opposed Thrasea. Tacitus says most laughed at the comparison.

settings.what: Vitellius's first words about the revolt
settings.to: the soldiers
settings.when: when he heard of the 3rd legion's revolt
settings.why: To deny any danger of civil war, blame the dismissed Praetorians for rumors and keep Vespasian's name quiet.

settings.what: Tacitus on the sources for this war
settings.to: his readers
settings.when: after the account of Caecina's and Bassus's turn
settings.why: To say that the writers of the Flavian years twisted the reasons into flattery, and to give his own reading: rivalry and envy of others who might get ahead of them in Vitellius's favor.

traditions.q: How much of the Olivet Discourse did the war of AD 66-70 fulfill?
views: The Catechism speaks of Christ's coming in glory as still ahead, preceded by a final trial of the Church in which the supreme deception is the Antichrist (Catechism 673, 675, 677). Those paragraphs do not discuss AD 70.

Mostly future, with the Roman war as a first fulfillment. John Chrysostom, whom the Orthodox Church honors, read the "wars and reports of wars" of Matthew 24:6 as the Jewish wars coming on Jerusalem (Homilies on Matthew 75) and the later signs as marks of Christ's second coming and the Antichrist (Homilies on Matthew 76).

Divided. Many Reformed and Presbyterian writers today are partial preterists, reading most of the discourse as fulfilled in AD 70 and the rest as the final return (R. C. Sproul, Kenneth Gentry). Full preterism, which says the return has already happened, is rejected by Reformed churches.
Future. Matthew 24 describes the seven-year tribulation, centered on Israel, and "this generation" is the generation alive when the signs begin.
